newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo tourism faces tough return to world markets.
newsitem.headline: Yugo tourism faces tough return to world markets.

text.p: Yugoslavia's tourism industry is in dire straits and faces an awesome struggle to regain its place on the world market after years of isolation and current political instability, industry sources said on Tuesday.
"We face a very tough struggle with both old and new competitors to return to foreign tour operators' programmes," said Serbia's Tourist Organisation director Jovan Popesku.

Popesku was opening the first international tourism fair since an international trade embargo on Serbia and Montenegro was lifted last October, but the only foreigners to attend were from Yugoslavia's southern neighbour Macedonia and Greece.
"Yugoslavia has registered an encouraging 39 percent growth in foreign visitors since sanctions were suspended (in 1995) and later lifted," Popesku said.
Wars and 3-1/2 year sanctions coupled with mismanagement and corruption brought Yugoslavia's economy to a virtual standstill, with export-oriented industry hit the hardest.
The tourism industry relied largely on Yugoslav tourists for survival but their numbers dwindled too amid plummeting standards of living.
Three months of massive demonstrations and political turmoil over local election fraud in Serbia since November further hurt the industry, halving the number of visitors in January from December.
Industry officials have asked the government for financial support to help upgrade decayed facilities and to promote Yugoslav tourism abroad.
"Tourism has great potential but above all we must raise quality, which requires new development and investment support," Popesku said.
But securing funds in Yugoslavia's cash-strapped economy will be very difficult.
Montenegro, which has a much bigger tourism industry than Serbia thanks to its access to the Adriatic sea, has launched plans to privatise hotels in an effort to secure funds.
But despite its efforts it has failed to attract major foreign investors wary of the political instability.

"We must have a clear idea where we are and what we expect of tourism, because it is very important for the economy and society as a whole," Popesku said, echoing the industry's calls to the government for a long-term development strategy.
The number of tourists in Yugoslavia in 1996 dropped 6.6 percent against 1995 to 2.85 million. Yugoslavs accounted for 2.55 million of the total, a drop of 9.8 percent on the previous year.
"Sales on the local market are down because people just do not have the money any more," one tour operator told Reuters.
The average monthly wage in Yugoslavia in February was barely over $100, close to subsistence level.
Foreign visitors' numbers jumped 62.8 percent in 1996 against 1995 to reach 162,109, but this was still just a fraction of the figures for Serbia and Montenegro before 1991.
According to central bank figures, hard currency income from tourism in January-November 1996 period was $40.2 million, or 7.8 percent more than in the same 11-month period in 1995.

"Although our efforts are aimed at the foreign market, Yugoslav tourists will remain the backbone of development this as well as next year," Popesku said. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
